name: microduck
readmeExcerpt:
Microduck

A tiny biped robot that moves using reinforcement learning policies.

Get yours here · Cheat sheet · Training the policies · How it works · Contributing

--- **This repo is the duck's brain.** About 25 cm and 800 g of robot, run by a handful of daemons on a Rockchip RK3566: a 50 Hz control loop driving fifteen servos from neural policies, the radios and the camera, and the update machinery that gets new software onto a robot without bricking it. Everything you need to run a Microduck is here. **If you want one, [get yours here](https://pollen-robotics.com/microduck).** The policies it runs are trained next door, in **[microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl)** — MuJoCo and PPO, the sim2real recipe, and the export to ONNX that this repo loads. ## It does things
It walks. Pick up a gamepad and drive. It rolls. Put wheels on, ask for roller mode, and it loads the other brain.
It picks things up. Beak to the floor, one button. It gets back up. Knock it over and it stands itself up.
It also sits, kicks a ball, rolls forward on command, and quacks in a voice that is its own. ## Where to find things ### You have a duck | | | |---|---| | [Cheat sheet](docs/robot/cheatsheet.md) | Every `robotctl` command: drive, configure, voice, chorale, theremin, wifi, updates, logs. Start here. | | [Gamepad](docs/robot/cheatsheet.md#gamepad-configd) | The full button mapping, and pairing a pad — [once per pad](docs/robot/pair-a-gamepad.md), plus what to do when it will not bond. | | [`duckctl`](docs/robot/duckctl.md) | The robot from a laptop over Bluetooth, with no network and no ssh. | | [Updates](docs/robot/cheatsheet.md#updates-updaterd) | Install, roll back, pin. Every update is verified, health-gated and reversible. | ### You are building on it | | | |---|---| | [microduck_rl](https://github.com/pollen-robotics/microduck_rl) | Where the policies come from: MuJoCo, PPO, domain randomisation, and the ONNX export this repo loads. | | [How it works](docs/design/architecture.md) | The whole system on one page — the daemons, the bus, how an update reaches a robot — then a page per part. | | [Set up a dev board](docs/robot/install-dev.md) | From a blank board to a robot that takes branch builds. | | [Dev cheat sheet](docs/robot/cheatsheet-dev.md) | Branch builds, release candidates, driving from a laptop, and the restart traps after an update. | | [Push your branch](docs/robot/dev-push.md) | Build on your machine, install over ssh, about a minute. | | [The simulated duck](docs/robot/simulation.md) | No robot on the desk? `scripts/duck-sim` runs the real daemons against a body in MuJoCo — one duck in a window, or four as machines you log into. | | [CONTRIBUTING.md](CONTRIBUTING.md) | Building, testing, layout, conventions, releasing. | | [Docs index](docs/README.md) | Everything, including the design pages and the open problems. | ## Under the hood Rust, no framework, one workspace. `robotd` owns the control loop and the motor bus; `updaterd` installs signed releases and rolls them back when a robot comes up unhealthy; `configd` owns wifi and identity; `btd` is the Bluetooth path a phone uses; `padd` reads the gamepad; `mediad` streams the camera over WebRTC; `tofd` serves the depth sensor. They talk over one JSON-RPC contract on Unix sockets, and every client — the app, the console, the gamepad, your script — sends exactly the same calls. The interesting decisions are written down: [`docs/design/`](docs/design/) is why things are the way they are, and [`docs/project/`](docs/project/) is what has gone wrong and what would close it. ## A note on ducks No duck was harmed in the making of this robot. Several were consulted.
readmeHtml:
Microduck

A tiny biped robot that moves using reinforcement learning policies.

Get yours here · Cheat sheet · Training the policies · How it works · Contributing

This repo is the duck's brain. About 25 cm and 800 g of robot, run by a handful of daemons on a Rockchip RK3566: a 50 Hz control loop driving fifteen servos from neural policies, the radios and the camera, and the update machinery that gets new software onto a robot without bricking it.

Everything you need to run a Microduck is here. If you want one, get yours here.

The policies it runs are trained next door, in microduck_rl — MuJoCo and PPO, the sim2real recipe, and the export to ONNX that this repo loads.

It does things

walk.MP4
roller_cut.mp4
It walks. Pick up a gamepad and drive. It rolls. Put wheels on, ask for roller mode, and it loads the other brain.
grasp.MP4
standup.MP4
It picks things up. Beak to the floor, one button. It gets back up. Knock it over and it stands itself up.

It also sits, kicks a ball, rolls forward on command, and quacks in a voice that is its own.

Where to find things

You have a duck
Cheat sheet Every robotctl command: drive, configure, voice, chorale, theremin, wifi, updates, logs. Start here.
Gamepad The full button mapping, and pairing a pad — once per pad, plus what to do when it will not bond.
duckctl The robot from a laptop over Bluetooth, with no network and no ssh.
Updates Install, roll back, pin. Every update is verified, health-gated and reversible.

You are building on it
microduck_rl Where the policies come from: MuJoCo, PPO, domain randomisation, and the ONNX export this repo loads.
How it works The whole system on one page — the daemons, the bus, how an update reaches a robot — then a page per part.
Set up a dev board From a blank board to a robot that takes branch builds.
Dev cheat sheet Branch builds, release candidates, driving from a laptop, and the restart traps after an update.
Push your branch Build on your machine, install over ssh, about a minute.
The simulated duck No robot on the desk? scripts/duck-sim runs the real daemons against a body in MuJoCo — one duck in a window, or four as machines you log into.
CONTRIBUTING.md Building, testing, layout, conventions, releasing.
Docs index Everything, including the design pages and the open problems.

Under the hood

Rust, no framework, one workspace. robotd owns the control loop and the motor bus; updaterd installs signed releases and rolls them back when a robot comes up unhealthy; configd owns wifi and identity; btd is the Bluetooth path a phone uses; padd reads the gamepad; mediad streams the camera over WebRTC; tofd serves the depth sensor. They talk over one JSON-RPC contract on Unix sockets, and every client — the app, the console, the gamepad, your script — sends exactly the same calls.

The interesting decisions are written down: docs/design/ is why things are the way they are, and docs/project/ is what has gone wrong and what would close it.

A note on ducks

No duck was harmed in the making of this robot. Several were consulted.

releases.name: daemon 0.18.5-dev.1577.a5b69ed (stress-test)
releases.body:
Dev build of `stress-test` at `a5b69ed07230517cf5fe5802f9302d84488227ac`.

Install on a **dev board**:

```
sudo robotctl update apply daemon --ref stress-test
```

Signed with `team.dev`, so a customer robot refuses it. Make a board a dev
board once with `sudo robotctl configure --allow-dev-daemon on` — see
docs/robot/install-dev.md.

`duckctl` from this branch, on Linux or macOS:

```
curl -fsSL https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pollen-robotics/microduck/main/scripts/install-duckctl.sh | sh -s -- stress-test
```

On Windows, `duckctl-windows-x86_64.zip` below — docs/robot/duckctl.md has the steps.

This tag moves on every push to the branch; the version inside does not.

aiSummary.oneLiner: A tiny bipedal robot controlled by reinforcement learning policies running on a Rockchip RK3566.
aiSummary.whatItDoes: The Microduck repository serves as the core brain for a 25 cm, 800 g bipedal robot. It runs a 50 Hz control loop driving fifteen servos via neural policies exported to ONNX from a separate reinforcement learning repository. It manages the hardware daemons for the servos, radios, camera, and safe over-the-air software updates. The system allows the robot to walk, roll on wheels, pick up items, and stand up automatically after falling. Users can control it directly using a paired gamepad or through Bluetooth commands without needing a network connection.
keyFeatures: Neural policy execution: Load ONNX models trained with MuJoCo and PPO to control fifteen servos.
Hardware abstraction: Manage radios, camera input, and a 50 Hz control loop on a Rockchip RK3566.
Safe software updates: Deploy new branch builds or releases over the air with rollback protection.
Dual locomotion modes: Switch between bipedal walking and rolling depending on the installed feet.
Local bluetooth control: Drive the robot directly from a laptop using the duckctl command-line tool.

useCases.title: Deploying custom firmwares
useCases.description: Build branch updates locally and install them over ssh in about a minute.

useCases.title: Operating without network
useCases.description: Pair a standard gamepad directly to drive the robot in isolated environments.

useCases.title: Executing complex maneuvers
useCases.description: Trigger pre-programmed behaviors like sitting, kicking, or standing up after a fall.

aiSummary.whoIsItFor: This repository is designed for roboticists and researchers interested in deploying reinforcement learning models onto physical hardware. Users need access to a physical Microduck robot or the included MuJoCo simulation tools to run the software.
